body.text:
**Your first tangible artifact is ready — open this in your browser:**

```
C:\src\git-for-ai\.git-for-ai\report.html
```

It's the agent-activity digest for this very repo, generated from the real data: **17 commits, 12 changes, 11 agent-authored / 1 human (your plan approval), 9 captured sessions, 2 models** (`claude-fable-5` and `claude-sonnet-5`). You'll see the timeline with confidence and risk badges, and each change's detail card pairing the claim with its evidence — what was tested, what files were in scope, and the session capture line underneath. Honest amber tags mark the early commits that predate capture; nothing is faked. It's fully self-contained (no scripts, no network), adapts to dark/light mode, and I verified its reads leave the repo's data byte-for-byte untouched.

All 10 of its tests passed on my independent re-run, and the command logic is committed (`74a73f3`). The `git for-ai report` CLI wiring lands as soon as the M10 agent — still finishing its real-model reindex dogfood — releases `bin.ts`; then `git for-ai report` regenerates this page any time, with `--since`/`--md` options.

This page is the seed of the review UI you approved: same information design, static first. When M11/M12 land, the interactive SPA adds search and "why?" navigation on top. But this is the "prove it to me" surface, version one — go have a look.

Yes, with one caveat. The likely RAM hog is the M10 agent's real-model reindex run — a Node process holding the ~1–2 GB ONNX embedding model while it indexes this repo. Killing it aborts that dogfood run, **but it's cheap to abort**: the embedding cache writes each vector atomically as it goes, so everything already embedded is kept, and a rerun resumes from cache instead of starting over. There may also be a few leftover vitest worker processes from the test runs, which are pure waste and always safe to kill.

So go ahead:

```powershell
Get-Process node | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object Id, @{n='RAM(MB)';e={[int]($_.WS/1MB)}}, StartTime
```

to see them, and `Stop-Process -Id <pid>` for the big ones (or `Get-Process node | Stop-Process` to clear the lot — my own tool processes respawn per command, so you won't break this session).

If you kill the reindex run, tell me and I'll have the M10 agent redo the dogfood afterward — with the model download done and the cache primed, the rerun will be far quicker and lighter than the first pass. Your `report.html` is unaffected either way — it's already generated and committed logic; only the `bin.ts` wiring waits on M10.

attributes.command: echo "- [RAM limit for spawned processes](ram-limit-5gb.md) — keep under ~5GB total; never run the embedder concurrently with other heavy work" >> "C:\Users\Hurricane\.claude\projects\C--src-git-for-ai\memory\MEMORY.md"

body.text:
Understood, and I've saved it as a permanent rule for this project: **spawned work stays under ~5GB total RAM.** Concretely, that means:

1. **No parallel heavy workloads** — the real lever. The embedding model (the current hog) will never again run at the same time as a full test suite or a second heavy agent; those get sequenced from now on. Today's squeeze came precisely from the M10 dogfood running while other verification was happening.
2. **Heap caps on spawned Node processes** (`--max-old-space-size`) where they help — with the honest caveat that the ONNX model weights are native memory, so the only true control for the model itself is running it alone and letting it finish.
3. **Milestone agent briefs will carry the constraint** whenever their work touches the embedder or big test runs.

The current reindex run gets to finish as you decided — it's a one-time cost (model download + first full index), and every future pass rides the cache at a fraction of the memory and time. Once it completes and the M10 agent reports, I'll verify, commit, wire `report` and `reindex` into the CLI together, and then `git for-ai report` is yours to run any time.

body.text:
It's broken — or at least producing nothing. The evidence after nearly an hour:

- **Zero vectors cached**: `.git-for-ai/embcache/` is completely empty, and every embedded chunk should be writing a cache file as it lands.
- **State untouched**: `state.json` still says `chunk_count: 0`, `last_indexed_commit: null`, last updated *yesterday* — the run has never checkpointed anything.
- Node processes exist (one started 5:04 PM, two from ~3:49 PM), but with no output artifacts whatsoever, they're either hung on the model download/load or deadlocked before the first embed.

A healthy first run would have shown cache files accumulating within minutes of the model loading. An hour with literally zero progress artifacts means it's stalled, not slow.

My recommendation: kill the Node processes (in PowerShell: `Get-Process node | Stop-Process`) — nothing of value is lost, since nothing was ever written — and I'll resume the M10 agent with instructions to rerun the dogfood **with verbose logging to a file and a watchdog**, so if it stalls again we see exactly where (model download vs. load vs. first inference). The likely culprits are a stalled HuggingFace download on this connection or the model loading in a subprocess whose stdout nobody is draining; both are diagnosable in one instrumented rerun, and both have straightforward fixes (pre-fetching the model file explicitly, or piping output properly).

Say the word and I'll kill them and relaunch it instrumented — or kill them yourself and just tell me when done.

The M10 agent is resumed with a proper diagnostic protocol this time: first check whether the 162 MB model file ever actually finished downloading to wherever its new durable cache location points (my leading suspect — if it relocated the cache away from where M9's run downloaded the model, it would have been re-downloading from scratch, possibly stalling), then rerun with all output logged to a file, polling checks on the log and cache, and a hard 10-minute no-progress timeout so it kills and reports rather than hanging silently again. It also carries your RAM rule: nothing else heavy runs alongside the model.

Either way we get a definitive answer this time — a completed dogfood with real numbers, or the exact stall point from the log plus a proposed fix. I'll report as soon as it comes back.

The instrumented rerun is now underway — the agent launched it with the watchdog and completion monitors armed, and it will be re-woken automatically by its own progress checks rather than sitting blind like last time. The 10-minute no-progress tripwire means the maximum time to a definitive answer is short: either cache files start appearing and the run completes with real numbers, or it gets killed at the stall point and we see exactly what hung from the log.

No action needed from you — your machine should stay responsive this time (single model process, nothing else heavy running). I'll report the moment it comes back with either the completed dogfood or the diagnosis.
